4.text: Compounds that release more than ΔG°′ ≈ −30 kJ/mol on hydrolysis are called **high-energy (macroergic)** compounds; such a bond is shown with the ∼ symbol. ATP is a high-energy compound for three reasons: **mutual repulsion of the negative charges** of the phosphate groups, **resonance stabilization** of the products (ADP and phosphate) and their better **hydration**.

head: Compound
ΔG°′, kJ/mol

4.text: ATP stands in the middle of the table: that is why it is synthesized by **accepting** phosphate from higher-energy compounds (phosphoenolpyruvate, creatine phosphate) and **donates** it to lower-energy compounds (glucose, glycerol). **Creatine phosphate** is the ATP reserve of muscle: with creatine kinase it regenerates ATP from ADP instantly and supplies the first 10 seconds of a short intense effort.

The actual ΔG in the cell differs from the standard value because the concentrations of substances are not 1 mol/L: ΔG = ΔG°′ + R·T·ln([ADP]·[P~i~] / [ATP]). Since [ATP] in the cell is much higher than ADP, the actual ΔG of ATP hydrolysis reaches **−50 to −60 kJ/mol**.

6.text: The **Mifflin–St Jeor formula** is used to estimate the basal metabolic rate (mass in kg, height in cm, age in years, result in kcal/day): for men BMR = 10·mass + 6.25·height − 5·age + 5; for women BMR = 10·mass + 6.25·height − 5·age − 161. Total expenditure is found by multiplying the BMR by a **physical activity factor**: sedentary — 1.2, moderate — 1.55, high — 1.9.

The **specific dynamic action of food** is the extra energy spent on digesting and absorbing food: ≈ 30 % of the energy consumed for proteins, 5–10 % for carbohydrates and 2–5 % for fats. That is why body temperature and heat production rise more after a protein meal.

parts.text: The mitochondria of **brown adipose tissue** (abundant in newborns) contain the protein **thermogenin** (UCP1): it “dissipates” the proton gradient without ATP synthesis and converts the energy of oxidation entirely into heat. This is non-shivering thermogenesis, which protects the newborn from cold.

blocks.text: The state of a reversible reaction in which the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal is called **chemical equilibrium**. For the reaction aA + bB ⇄ cC + dD the **equilibrium constant** (law of mass action) is: K = [C]^c^·[D]^d^ / ([A]^a^·[B]^b^). If K > 1, the equilibrium lies on the side of the products.

The equilibrium constant is related to the standard Gibbs energy: ΔG° = −R·T·lnK. At 298 K, if K = 10, then ΔG° ≈ −5.7 kJ/mol; every 10-fold increase in K lowers ΔG° by another 5.7 kJ/mol. Reactions with a negative ΔG° lie mainly on the product side at equilibrium.
**Le Chatelier’s principle:** if an external influence is applied to a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces this influence.

parts.text: In carbon monoxide poisoning the equilibrium HbCO + O~2~ ⇄ HbO~2~ + CO is governed by Le Chatelier’s principle: 100 % oxygen, especially under high pressure in a hyperbaric chamber, shifts the equilibrium **to the right** and displaces CO from hemoglobin faster.

insert.title: 0. Fundamentals of chemical kinetics and catalysis

blocks.text: Thermodynamics answers the question of whether a reaction **can occur**, while **chemical kinetics** studies **how fast** it occurs. For example, the oxidation of glucose by oxygen is very exergonic, yet sugar stays unchanged in a jar for years — the reaction rate is extremely small.

items: **Law of mass action (for rate):** v = k·[A]^a^·[B]^b^, where k is the rate constant.
**Van’t Hoff rule:** when the temperature rises by 10 °C, the rate of most reactions increases 2–4 times: v~2~ / v~1~ = γ^(t2 − t1) / 10^.
**Arrhenius equation:** k = A·e^−Ea / (RT)^; the rate depends sharply on the **activation energy** E~a~ — the energy barrier that must be overcome for the reaction to occur.

A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction by opening another pathway with a lower activation energy, but it does not change ΔH, ΔG or the position of equilibrium — it only helps the equilibrium to be reached faster.

blocks.text: **Enzymes** are biological catalysts. They speed up reactions 10^6^–10^12^ times, have high **specificity** and work under mild conditions (37 °C, pH ≈ 7). An enzyme forms an **enzyme–substrate complex** with the substrate: E + S ⇄ ES → E + P. Michaelis–Menten equation: v = V~max~·[S] / (K~m~ + [S]), where K~m~ is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half the maximum.

parts.text: The van’t Hoff rule is also seen in the clinic: when body temperature rises by 1 °C, metabolism and oxygen consumption increase by about 10–13 % — in fever the heart rate and breathing speed up. Conversely, **hypothermia** slows metabolism; that is why artificial cooling is used during heart surgery and after cardiac arrest to protect the brain.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: For the denaturation of a protein ΔH = +400 kJ/mol and ΔS = +1.2 kJ/(mol·K).
cases.ask: Calculate ΔG at 37 °C and 70 °C. Above what temperature does the protein denature spontaneously?
cases.answer: 37 °C (310 K): ΔG = 400 − 310 · 1.2 = 400 − 372 = **+28 kJ/mol** — denaturation is not spontaneous, the protein is stable. 70 °C (343 K): ΔG = 400 − 343 · 1.2 = 400 − 411.6 = **−11.6 kJ/mol** — denaturation is spontaneous. Equilibrium temperature: T = ΔH / ΔS = 400 / 1.2 ≈ 333 K = **60 °C**. That is why high temperature destroys microbial proteins in pasteurization and sterilization, while a fever above 42 °C is dangerous for the body.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: The equilibrium constant of an enzymatic reaction at 25 °C is K = 1000.
cases.ask: Calculate the standard Gibbs energy of the reaction (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)). Which side does the equilibrium lie on?
cases.answer: ΔG° = −R·T·lnK = −8.314 · 298 · ln1000 = −8.314 · 298 · 6.91 ≈ −17 100 J/mol = **−17.1 kJ/mol**. ΔG° is negative and K is large — at equilibrium the **products** predominate: for every 1000 product molecules there is only 1 molecule of starting substance.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A 20-year-old student: mass 70 kg, height 175 cm, moderately physically active (factor 1.55).
cases.ask: Calculate the basal metabolic rate and daily energy expenditure using the Mifflin–St Jeor formula.
cases.answer: BMR = 10 · 70 + 6.25 · 175 − 5 · 20 + 5 = 700 + 1093.75 − 100 + 5 ≈ **1699 kcal/day**. Total expenditure = 1699 · 1.55 ≈ **2633 kcal/day** (≈ 11 000 kJ). To keep the weight stable, the energy value of the diet should equal this.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A patient’s body temperature rose from 37 °C to 40 °C. Take the temperature coefficient of metabolic reactions as γ = 2.
cases.ask: How many times does the reaction rate increase according to the van’t Hoff rule? What does this mean clinically?
cases.answer: v~2~ / v~1~ = 2^(40 − 37) / 10^ = 2^0.3^ ≈ **1.23** — reactions speed up by ≈ 23 %. In fever oxygen consumption and CO~2~ production increase, so the heart rate and breathing speed up; in patients with heart or lung disease this extra load can be dangerous. That is why antipyretics are given for high fever.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: An overweight patient reduced the diet by 500 kcal a day to lose weight; physical activity did not change. 1 kg of adipose tissue ≈ 7700 kcal.
cases.ask: How many days are needed to lose 1 kg of adipose tissue? About how much weight loss can be expected in a month?
cases.answer: 7700 / 500 ≈ **15 days** per 1 kg. In a month (30 days) about 30 · 500 / 7700 ≈ **2 kg**. This is a safe and sustainable rate of weight loss; severe starvation, in contrast, leads to the breakdown of muscle proteins and a fall in the basal metabolic rate. The thermodynamic basis of weight loss is the law of conservation of energy: if expenditure exceeds intake, the missing energy is taken from the oxidation of stored fat.
